summary: Describes an optimization for OSPF database exchange in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. A router skips listing an LSA in Database Description packets if the neighbor already listed the same or a newer instance. It stays compatible and cuts overhead by about half in large networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When OSPF routers compare their databases, they can avoid listing information the neighbor already has. This reduces repeated data during database exchange without changing synchronization.

questions: what is the ospf database exchange optimization
what is a database description packet
what is an ospf database description packet
subtitle: A backward-compatible way to send fewer OSPF database summary headers.

tldr.problem: During database exchange, neighboring OSPF routers can list LSA headers that the other router already has.
tldr.mechanism: A router removes a summary entry when the neighbor's Database Description packet already listed the same or a more recent LSA.
tldr.outcome: The optimization reduces Database Description overhead by about 50% in large, nearly synchronized networks. RFC 9454 later updated this memo.

today: RFC 5243 is Informational and was updated by RFC 9454. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: The Database Exchange Optimization
sections.content:
When neighboring OSPF routers become adjacent, they synchronize their link-state databases through Database Description (DD) packets. Each packet lists link-state advertisement (LSA) headers so a router can tell whether its neighbor has newer information to request.

A router need not list an LSA if the neighbor already has the same or a more recent instance. The neighbor's DD packet shows this. The router then removes that LSA from the neighbor's Database summary list.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can skip describing an LSA when its neighbor has already listed the same or a newer copy. The neighbor's own packet tells it which entries to remove from its summary.

sections.title: Updating the Summary List
sections.content:
When a router accepts the next Database Description packet, it checks each listed LSA. If its own database has no copy or has an older copy, the LSA is added to the Link State Request list. If the Database summary list contains an instance that is the same as or less recent than the one listed by the neighbor, that summary entry is removed.

The removal may happen before or after the database lookup, but it must be done for every LSA in the received packet before the router sends its next DD packet in response. The RFC recommends a common increasing order for LSAs to make lookups faster, with a different field order for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.
sections.plainLanguage: For each LSA in the neighbor's packet, the router requests it only if its own copy is missing or older. It crosses off entries the neighbor already has before sending its next packet.

sections.title: Example and Effects
sections.content:
The example starts with RT1 and RT2 holding identical databases whose LSA headers fit in two DD packets. Without the optimization, each router sends two full DD packets. With it, each sends one full DD packet because it removes headers already listed by the neighbor.

The RFC says the change is backward compatible and does not affect synchronization, since it omits only unnecessary information. It can reduce the number of LSA headers exchanged by about half in large networks where routers are usually nearly synchronized when they become adjacent, and is especially useful where bandwidth is limited.
sections.plainLanguage: In the example, each router sends one full packet instead of two. The RFC says this saves repeated headers without changing how the databases synchronize.
